name: Fat grafting for facial asymmetry

lead: Fat grafting harvests a patient's own fat, usually by liposuction, processes it and injects it into areas lacking volume. For asymmetry, the payoff is a visibly fuller, more even face once the thinner side is built up to match.

The fat is washed or filtered and re-injected into the target area. Facial fat grafting is widely used in reconstructive and cosmetic surgery. A systematic review reports that a main drawback is high and unpredictable absorption, so surgeons judge retention from experience; the studies reviewed concern facial volume restoration in general rather than asymmetry specifically.

paras: It is done by a surgeon, often under sedation or anaesthesia, with fat taken from areas such as the abdomen or thighs. Swelling settles over weeks and the final volume shows after some of the graft is absorbed. Because retention varies, some patients have repeat sessions.

Reported problems include swelling, bruising, contour irregularities, infection, fat necrosis and reabsorption; a systematic review asks whether facial fat grafting is worth its risk. Results may need touch-ups.

angle.text: Surgeons move a patient's own fat into the thinner side of the face so the two sides match in volume, giving a visibly fuller, more balanced face. Fat transfer is a standard reconstructive and aesthetic technique, with graft survival varying between patients.

lead: Fat grafting, or fat transfer, moves a person's own fat from one area to another. It has three stages: harvesting, usually by liposuction, processing, and reinjection.[1] It is used in reconstructive and aesthetic surgery for volume replacement, including the face.[1][2]

Fat grafting for facial asymmetry refers to using the technique to add volume to a deficient side so the two sides match. A systematic review reports that the main drawbacks of facial autologous fat grafting are high absorption and unpredictable volume retention.[3]

paras: Fat grafting is performed under general or local anaesthesia. Facial uses include restoring volume to deflated compartments and improving contour around the eyes and mouth.[1] Soft-tissue volume loss is considered a key component of facial aging, and fillers and fat are used to address it.[4]

A systematic review and meta-analysis examined volume retention after facial fat grafting and the factors that influence it, noting that surgeons have usually relied on their own experience.[3] Trials have compared fat processing methods, including filtered and washed versus centrifuged fat in 25 healthy patients, and a randomized trial using three-dimensional volumetric analysis of three processing techniques.[5][6] Wikipedia notes that the body may reabsorb a substantial share of grafted fat in breast augmentation and that weight change can affect results.[1]

Reported complications include swelling, bruising, hematoma, nerve sensation changes, hypertrophic scarring, infection, contour irregularities, fat necrosis and reabsorption.[1] A 2022 systematic review of complications of facial fat grafting asks whether the procedure is worth the risk.[7]

Studies exist of facial fat grafting in general, including volume retention, processing methods and complications.[3][5][6][7] Registered trials cover facial uses such as skin texture and facial trauma.[8][9] No studies found specifically on fat grafting for facial asymmetry framed as looksmaxxing.
